\section[\ar{أب} \ar{أم}]{\ar{أب}, \ar{أم} (ab, umm) — father and mother}

\label{lesson:AR-C10-ab-umm}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Two short, ancient words — each just two or three letters — sitting at the root of Semitic family vocabulary across several languages, not just Arabic.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أب}} (\emph{ab}) = "\textbf{father}." A short, ancient Semitic root, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{אב}} (\emph{av}) and Aramaic \textbf{\he{אבא}} (\emph{abba}) — the very word behind "\textbf{Abba, Father}" in the New Testament.
  \item \textbf{\ar{أم}} (\emph{umm}) = "\textbf{mother}." Equally ancient, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{אם}} (\emph{em}).
\end{itemize}

These aren't borrowings between Arabic and Hebrew — both descend from the same ancient Semitic family vocabulary, the way \emph{pater} and English \emph{father} are cousins through PIE rather than one copying the other.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ar{أم}} stays productive in everyday Arabic naming: \textbf{\ar{أم}} + a child's name forms a \textbf{kunya}, an honorific "\textbf{mother of \_\_\_}" (and \textbf{\ar{أبو}}, \emph{abū}, does the same for fathers — "\textbf{father of \_\_\_}"). Someone might be known publicly as \emph{Umm Khālid}, "mother of Khālid," rather than by their own given name — a naming custom still very much alive today.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ab" — father — then "umm," mother{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the Hebrew cousins — "ab/av, umm/em"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the naming pattern — "Umm + {[}child's name{]}" = mother of \_\_\_{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What are Arabic's words for father and mother? (\textbf{\ar{أب} ab, \ar{أم} umm}.) What are their Hebrew cousins? (\textbf{av, em} — not borrowings, both from the same ancient Semitic root.) What naming pattern does \textbf{umm} still form today? (\textbf{Umm + {[}child's name{]}}, "mother of \_\_\_," a living honorific.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{أخ} \ar{أخت}]{\ar{أخ}, \ar{أخت} (akh, ukht) — brother and sister}

\label{lesson:AR-C10-akh-ukht}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Unlike the color words you just learned (a whole reshaped template for masculine/feminine), siblings here use the \textbf{simplest} possible gender marker.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أخ}} (\emph{akh}) = "\textbf{brother}" — another short, ancient Semitic root, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{אח}} (\emph{ach}).
  \item \textbf{\ar{أخت}} (\emph{ukht}) = "\textbf{sister}" — the \textbf{same root}, plus a plain feminine \textbf{‑\ar{ت}} (\emph{‑t}) ending, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{אחות}} (\emph{achot}).
\end{itemize}

So \emph{ukht} isn't a separate word — it's \emph{akh} wearing the ordinary feminine ending, the simple pattern you already know from \textbf{\ar{آسف}/\ar{آسفة}} (\emph{āsif/āsifa}, "sorry"), not the elaborate colors template.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "akh" — brother — then "ukht," sister{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the shared root plus a simple ending — akh + ‑t{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the Hebrew cousins — "akh/ach, ukht/achot"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What are Arabic's words for brother and sister? (\textbf{\ar{أخ} akh, \ar{أخت} ukht}.) How is \emph{ukht} built from \emph{akh}? (\textbf{The same root, plus a plain feminine ‑\ar{ت} ending} — the simple pattern, not the colors' elaborate template.) What are their Hebrew cousins? (\textbf{ach, achot}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
